bookTitle: India and the Contemporary World – II

chapters.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
chapters.overview: The chapter traces how nationalism emerged in nineteenth-century Europe and replaced multi-national dynastic empires with nation-states. It follows the French Revolution and Napoleon, liberal nationalism and the conservative order after 1815, the revolutions of 1830-1848, the unification of Germany and Italy and the case of Britain, the visual personification of nations, and the link between nationalism and imperialism that led to the First World War.

sections.title: Nationalism in Europe
points: In 1848 the French artist Frédéric Sorrieu made a series of prints of a world of 'democratic and social Republics'; the first shows the peoples of Europe and America offering homage to the statue of Liberty.

In his utopian vision nations are identified by flags and national costume; the United States and Switzerland lead the procession, followed by France and Germany, whose peoples did not yet form a united nation.
During the nineteenth century nationalism brought the emergence of the nation-state in place of multi-national dynastic empires.
A nation-state is one in which the majority of citizens, not only rulers, develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent, forged through struggles.

Ernst Renan's 1882 lecture 'What is a Nation?' argued that a nation is not formed by common language, race, religion or territory but is a large-scale solidarity whose existence is a daily plebiscite.

sections.title: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation
points: The first clear expression of nationalism came with the French Revolution in 1789, which transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to the body of French citizens.
Revolutionaries created collective identity through the ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen), a new tricolour flag, and the Estates General renamed the National Assembly.

New hymns, oaths and martyrs, a centralised administration with uniform laws, abolition of internal customs duties, uniform weights and measures, and French as spoken in Paris as the common language were introduced.
The revolutionaries declared it the mission of the French nation to liberate the peoples of Europe from despotism; Jacobin clubs appeared and French armies carried nationalism abroad.
Napoleon destroyed democracy in France but through the Civil Code of 1804 (Napoleonic Code) abolished privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property.

In conquered regions he simplified administration, abolished feudalism and serfdom and removed guild restrictions, but increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription turned early enthusiasm into hostility.

sections.title: The Making of Nationalism in Europe
points: In mid-eighteenth-century Europe there were no nation-states; Germany, Italy and Switzerland were divided into kingdoms, duchies and cantons.
Eastern and Central Europe were under autocratic monarchies ruling diverse peoples who did not share a collective identity.
The Habsburg Empire over Austria-Hungary was a patchwork of regions and peoples whose only common tie was allegiance to the emperor.

subsections.title: The Aristocracy and the New Middle Class
points: A landed aristocracy, small in number, was the dominant class, united by a common way of life, speaking French in diplomacy and high society.
The majority were peasants; in the west land was farmed by tenants and small owners, while in Eastern and Central Europe vast estates were cultivated by serfs.
Industrialisation created a working class and middle classes of industrialists, businessmen and professionals.
Ideas of national unity following the abolition of aristocratic privileges gained popularity among the educated, liberal middle classes.

subsections.title: What did Liberal Nationalism Stand for?
points: Liberalism, from the Latin liber (free), stood for individual freedom, equality before the law, government by consent, a constitution, representative government and inviolability of private property.
Equality before the law did not mean universal suffrage: in revolutionary France only property-owning men could vote, and the Napoleonic Code reduced women to the status of a minor.
Economically, liberalism stood for freedom of markets and abolition of state restrictions on movement of goods and capital.
In the German confederation of 39 states, a merchant going from Hamburg to Nuremberg in 1833 passed 11 customs barriers, and the elle measure differed from region to region.
In 1834 a customs union (zollverein) formed at Prussia's initiative abolished tariff barriers and reduced currencies from over thirty to two; railways further stimulated economic nationalism.

subsections.title: A New Conservatism after 1815
points: After Napoleon's defeat conservatives sought to preserve monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family, while accepting that modernisation could strengthen monarchies.
In 1815 Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria met at Vienna, hosted by Duke Metternich, and drew up the Treaty of Vienna to undo the changes of the Napoleonic wars.
The Bourbon dynasty was restored, France lost annexed territories, and buffer states such as the Netherlands (including Belgium) were set up; Austria got northern Italy and Russia part of Poland.
The conservative regimes were autocratic and imposed censorship; liberal-nationalists took up freedom of the press.

subsections.title: The Revolutionaries
points: Fear of repression drove liberal-nationalists underground into secret societies that opposed the monarchies set up after the Vienna Congress.
Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1805 and a member of the Carbonari, was exiled in 1831 and founded Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne.
Mazzini believed nations were the natural units of mankind and Italy must be a single unified republic; Metternich called him 'the most dangerous enemy of our social order'.

sections.title: The Age of Revolutions: 1830-1848
points: Liberalism and nationalism became associated with revolutions led by the educated middle-class elite.

In July 1830 liberal revolutionaries in France overthrew the Bourbon kings and installed a constitutional monarchy under Louis Philippe; an uprising in Brussels led Belgium to break away from the Netherlands.
The Greek war of independence began in 1821 against the Ottoman Empire, supported by exiled Greeks and West Europeans; Lord Byron died in the war in 1824.
The Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation.

subsections.title: The Romantic Imagination and National Feeling
points: Culture – art, poetry, stories and music – helped express and shape nationalist feelings.
Romantic artists criticised the glorification of reason and science and focused on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings to create a shared cultural past.
Johann Gottfried Herder held that true German culture lay among the common people (das volk) and was popularised through folk songs, poetry and dances (volksgeist).
The Grimm brothers collected folktales, seeing them as expressions of a pure German spirit against French domination.

In partitioned Poland national feeling was kept alive through music (Karol Kurpinski's operas, the polonaise and mazurka) and the Polish language, used by clergy as a weapon against Russian dominance.

subsections.title: Hunger, Hardship and Popular Revolt
points: The 1830s were years of great economic hardship: population rose, jobs were scarce, rural migrants crowded into city slums, and small producers faced cheap machine-made imports from England.
Peasants bore feudal dues, and rising food prices or bad harvests led to widespread pauperism.

In 1848 food shortages and unemployment led Parisians to erect barricades; Louis Philippe fled and a National Assembly proclaimed a Republic, gave suffrage to adult males above 21 and set up national workshops.
In 1845 Silesian weavers revolted against contractors who drastically reduced payments; eleven weavers were shot.

subsections.title: 1848: The Revolution of the Liberals
points: Alongside the revolts of the poor, the educated middle classes combined demands for constitutionalism with national unification in Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

On 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives took their places in the Frankfurt parliament in the Church of St Paul and drafted a constitution for a German nation under a monarchy subject to parliament.
Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia rejected the crown; the middle-class parliament lost the support of workers and artisans and was forced to disband.
Women, though active in the liberal movement, were denied suffrage and admitted to the Frankfurt parliament only as observers in the gallery.
After 1848 monarchs granted concessions: serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and Russia, and Hungarians got more autonomy in 1867.

sections.title: The Making of Germany and Italy
points: After 1848 nationalism moved away from democracy and revolution and was often mobilised by conservatives to promote state power.

subsections.title: Germany – Can the Army be the Architect of a Nation?
points: The liberal initiative of 1848 was repressed by the monarchy and military supported by the Junkers (large landowners) of Prussia.
Prussia's chief minister Otto von Bismarck led unification with the Prussian army and bureaucracy; three wars over seven years with Austria, Denmark and France ended in Prussian victory.
On 18 January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
The new state modernised currency, banking, legal and judicial systems, and Prussian practices became a model for the rest of Germany.

subsections.title: Italy Unified
points: Italy was divided into seven states; only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house, the north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain.
After Mazzini's failed uprisings of 1831 and 1848, Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II took up unification through war.
Chief Minister Cavour, neither a revolutionary nor a democrat, engineered an alliance with France that defeated Austrian forces in 1859.
Garibaldi's armed volunteers marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860; in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.
Many illiterate peasants remained unaware of nationalist ideology and believed 'La Talia' was Victor Emmanuel's wife.

subsections.title: The Strange Case of Britain
points: In Britain the nation-state was the result of a long-drawn-out process, not a sudden revolution; earlier identities were English, Welsh, Scot or Irish.
The English parliament, which seized power from the monarchy in 1688, was the instrument that forged a nation-state with England at its centre.
The Act of Union (1707) formed the United Kingdom of Great Britain; Scotland's culture was suppressed and Highlanders were forbidden their Gaelic language and national dress.
Ireland, divided between Catholics and Protestants, was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom in 1801 after Wolfe Tone's failed revolt (1798).
A British nation was forged through a dominant English culture: the Union Jack, the national anthem and the English language.

sections.title: Visualising the Nation
points: Artists in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries personified nations as female figures, an allegory giving the abstract idea of the nation a concrete form.
During the French Revolution female allegories portrayed Liberty (red cap, broken chain), Justice (blindfolded woman with scales) and the Republic.
In France the nation was christened Marianne, with the red cap, tricolour and cockade; her statues stood in public squares and her image was on coins and stamps.
Germania became the allegory of the German nation, wearing a crown of oak leaves, as the German oak stands for heroism.
Box 3 explains symbols such as broken chains (being freed), sword (readiness to fight), olive branch (willingness to make peace) and rays of the rising sun (beginning of a new era).

sections.title: Nationalism and Imperialism
points: By the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism became a narrow creed with limited ends, and nationalist groups grew intolerant and ready for war.

The Balkans – modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, inhabited by Slavs – was the most serious source of tension after 1871.

The disintegration of the Ottoman Empire and romantic nationalism made the region explosive; Balkan states were jealous of each other and big powers (Russia, Germany, England, Austro-Hungary) competed there.
These rivalries led to a series of wars and finally the First World War in 1914.
Colonised countries developed anti-imperial nationalist movements, and the idea that societies should be organised into nation-states came to be accepted as natural and universal.

Relating to a common racial, tribal or cultural origin or background that a community identifies with or claims.

From the Latin liber, meaning free; for the middle classes it stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law.
A customs union formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia and joined by most German states.
The large landowners of Prussia.
The true spirit of the nation, which Herder said was popularised through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances.

chapters.title: Nationalism in India
chapters.overview: The chapter follows the Indian national movement from the 1920s, showing how modern nationalism grew out of the anti-colonial struggle. It covers the First World War, satyagraha, the Rowlatt Act, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, how towns, peasants, tribals and plantation workers understood swaraj, the Civil Disobedience Movement and its limits, and the cultural processes that created a sense of collective belonging.

sections.title: Nationalism in India
points: In India, as in many colonies, modern nationalism is intimately connected to the anti-colonial movement.
The sense of being oppressed under colonialism tied different groups together, though each experienced colonialism differently.
The Congress under Mahatma Gandhi tried to forge these groups into one movement, but unity did not emerge without conflict.

sections.title: The First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation
points: The war increased defence expenditure financed by war loans and taxes; customs duties were raised and income tax introduced.
Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, forced recruitment in villages caused anger, and crops failed in 1918-19 and 1920-21.
Famines and an influenza epidemic killed 12 to 13 million people according to the 1921 census.

subsections.title: The Idea of Satyagraha
points: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 from South Africa, where he had fought the racist regime through satyagraha.
Satyagraha emphasised the power of truth: if the cause was true and against injustice, physical force was unnecessary, and the oppressor's conscience could be appealed to through non-violence.
Gandhi organised satyagraha in Champaran, Bihar (1917) against the plantation system, among Ahmedabad cotton mill workers (1918), and for Kheda peasants (1918) who could not pay revenue.

subsections.title: The Rowlatt Act
points: The Rowlatt Act (1919), passed despite Indian members' opposition, allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years.
Gandhi called for a hartal on 6 April 1919; rallies, strikes and shop closures followed, and local leaders in Amritsar were arrested.
On 13 April General Dyer blocked the exits of Jallianwalla Bagh and fired on the crowd, killing hundreds, to 'produce a moral effect'.
Brutal repression followed; seeing violence spread, Gandhi called off the movement.

To bring Hindus and Muslims together Gandhi took up the Khilafat issue; a Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919, and at the Calcutta session in September 1920 he convinced leaders to start non-cooperation for Khilafat and swaraj.

subsections.title: Why Non-cooperation?
points: In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi argued that British rule survived only through Indian cooperation and would collapse within a year if Indians refused it.
The movement was to unfold in stages: surrender of titles, boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods, then full civil disobedience if repressed.
Many in the Congress were reluctant to boycott the November 1920 council elections and feared violence.
A compromise at the Nagpur session in December 1920 adopted the Non-Cooperation programme.

sections.title: Differing Strands within the Movement
points: The Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement began in January 1921.
Various social groups participated, each with its own aspiration; swaraj meant different things to different people.

subsections.title: The Movement in the Towns
points: Students left government schools, teachers resigned and lawyers gave up practice; council elections were boycotted except in Madras, where the Justice Party contested.
Foreign goods were boycotted and foreign cloth burnt; its import halved between 1921 and 1922, from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore, and Indian mill and handloom production rose.
The movement slowed because khadi was more expensive than mill cloth and alternative Indian institutions were slow to come up.

subsections.title: Rebellion in the Countryside
points: In Awadh, Baba Ramchandra led peasants against talukdars and landlords who demanded high rents, cesses and begar; peasants demanded reduced revenue, abolition of begar and social boycott of landlords.
The Oudh Kisan Sabha, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and others, was set up by October 1920 and had over 300 branches within a month.
In 1921 talukdars' houses were attacked and bazaars looted, in forms the Congress leadership was unhappy with.

In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, Alluri Sitaram Raju led a militant guerrilla movement against forest closures and begar, asserting India could be liberated only by force; he was executed in 1924.

subsections.title: Swaraj in the Plantations
points: Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859 Assam plantation workers could not leave the tea gardens without permission.
For them freedom meant moving freely and keeping a link with their villages; thousands left the plantations believing Gandhi Raj was coming.
Stranded by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught by police and brutally beaten.
Though these groups interpreted swaraj in their own ways, by invoking Gandhi they identified with an all-India movement.

sections.title: Towards Civil Disobedience
points: In February 1922 Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement as it was turning violent (Chauri Chaura).
C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party to return to council politics, while Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for radical agitation and full independence.
The worldwide depression made agricultural prices fall from 1926 and collapse after 1930.
The Simon Commission, with no Indian member, arrived in 1928 and was greeted with 'Go back Simon'; Lord Irwin offered vague 'dominion status' in October 1929.
In December 1929 the Lahore Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru formalised the demand for 'Purna Swaraj', and 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

subsections.title: The Salt March and the Civil Disobedience Movement
points: On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent Viceroy Irwin eleven demands, the most stirring being abolition of the salt tax, since salt was consumed by rich and poor alike.
Irwin would not negotiate, so Gandhi marched with 78 volunteers over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days and broke the salt law on 6 April by boiling sea water.
Unlike Non-Cooperation, people were now asked to break colonial laws: salt was made, foreign cloth boycotted, revenue and chaukidari taxes refused, and forest laws violated.
Arrests of leaders such as Abdul Ghaffar Khan led to violent clashes; about 100,000 people were arrested.

Gandhi called off the movement in the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931, went to the Round Table Conference in London in December 1931, relaunched the movement on return, and by 1934 it lost momentum.

subsections.title: How Participants saw the Movement
points: Rich peasants such as the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh, hit by falling prices, fought against high revenue and were disappointed when the movement was called off in 1931.
Poorer peasants wanted unpaid rent remitted and joined radical movements, but the Congress would not support 'no rent' campaigns.
Business classes formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920) and FICCI (1927), supported the movement at first, but became apprehensive after the Round Table Conference failed.
Industrial workers largely stayed aloof except in the Nagpur region, though there were strikes by railway workers (1930) and dockworkers (1932).
Women participated on a large scale, but Gandhi saw their duty as looking after home and hearth, and the Congress gave them little authority.

subsections.title: The Limits of Civil Disobedience
points: Gandhi called 'untouchables' harijan and campaigned against untouchability, but many dalit leaders sought reserved seats and separate electorates.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and demanded separate electorates at the second Round Table Conference; Gandhi began a fast unto death.
The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in legislative councils, voted in by the general electorate.
After the Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement declined, many Muslims felt alienated from the Congress, which became associated with Hindu religious nationalist groups like the Hindu Mahasabha.
Hopes of Congress-Muslim League unity faded at the All Parties Conference in 1928 when M.R. Jayakar opposed compromise, and many Muslims feared domination by a Hindu majority.

sections.title: The Sense of Collective Belonging
points: The sense of collective belonging came partly through united struggles and partly through history, fiction, folklore, songs, popular prints and symbols.

The identity of India came to be visually associated with Bharat Mata, first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who wrote 'Vande Mataram' in the 1870s; Abanindranath Tagore painted her as a calm, ascetic figure.
Nationalists recorded folk tales and songs; Rabindranath Tagore led folk revival in Bengal and Natesa Sastri published The Folklore of Southern India in Madras.
During the Swadeshi movement a red, green and yellow tricolour with eight lotuses and a crescent moon was designed; by 1921 Gandhi designed the Swaraj flag with a spinning wheel.
Nationalist histories glorified India's ancient achievements, but when the past and images celebrated were Hindu, other communities felt left out.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Growing anger against colonial rule brought various groups and classes together in a common struggle for freedom.
The Congress under Gandhi tried to channel grievances into organised movements, but groups participated with varied aspirations.
Unity often broke down as the Congress tried to ensure one group's demands did not alienate another; what emerged was a nation with many voices wanting freedom.
A box describes the Quit India Movement: the resolution was passed at Wardha on 14 July 1942 and endorsed in Bombay on 8 August 1942, when Gandhi gave the 'Do or Die' speech.

The refusal to deal and associate with people, participate in activities, or buy and use things; usually a form of protest.
A form of demonstration or protest by which people block the entrance to a shop, factory or office.
Labour that villagers were forced to contribute without any payment.
A method of mass agitation emphasising the power of truth and the need to search for truth, winning through non-violence by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.
Full independence for India, formalised as a demand by the Lahore Congress in December 1929.
The name, meaning children of God, Gandhi gave to the 'untouchables'.
Meaning oppressed; what the nation's 'untouchables' began to call themselves from around the 1930s.

chapters.title: The Making of a Global World
chapters.overview: The chapter shows that globalisation has a long history of trade, migration, movement of capital and exchange of ideas and diseases. It moves from the pre-modern world of silk routes and the conquest of America, through the nineteenth-century world economy, colonialism and indentured labour, to the inter-war economy and the Great Depression, and finally post-war reconstruction, the Bretton Woods institutions, decolonisation and the beginning of 'globalisation'.

sections.title: The Pre-modern World
points: The making of the global world has a long history of trade, migration, people in search of work and movement of capital.
Travellers, traders, priests and pilgrims carried goods, money, values, skills, ideas, inventions and even germs across vast distances.
As early as 3000 BCE coastal trade linked the Indus valley civilisations with present-day West Asia, and cowries from the Maldives reached China and East Africa.

subsections.title: Silk Routes Link the World
points: The silk routes, over land and by sea, linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa, existing from before the Christian Era almost till the fifteenth century.
Chinese silk and pottery and Indian and Southeast Asian textiles and spices travelled west, while gold and silver flowed from Europe to Asia.
Trade and cultural exchange went together: Christian missionaries, Muslim preachers and Buddhism travelled along these routes.

subsections.title: Food Travels: Spaghetti and Potato
points: Noodles may have travelled west from China to become spaghetti, or Arab traders may have taken pasta to fifth-century Sicily.
Potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes came to Europe and Asia only after Columbus reached the Americas.
Europe's poor ate better with the potato; when disease destroyed the potato crop in Ireland in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation.

subsections.title: Conquest, Disease and Trade
points: The world shrank in the sixteenth century after European sailors found a sea route to Asia and crossed to America; the Indian subcontinent had been central to Indian Ocean trade.
Silver from mines in present-day Peru and Mexico enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia.
The Portuguese and Spanish conquest of America was aided most by germs such as smallpox, to which the isolated inhabitants had no immunity.
Poverty, disease and religious persecution drove thousands from Europe to America, where slave plantations grew cotton and sugar for Europe.
China restricted overseas contact from the fifteenth century, and the centre of world trade moved westwards to Europe.

sections.title: The Nineteenth Century (1815-1914)
points: Economists identify three flows in international economic exchange: trade (largely in goods), labour (migration in search of work) and capital (investment over long distances).
The three flows were closely interwoven, though labour migration was often more restricted than goods or capital.

subsections.title: A World Economy Takes Shape
points: Population growth raised food prices in Britain, and the Corn Laws restricted the import of corn; industrialists and urban dwellers forced their abolition.
Cheap imports made British agriculture uncompetitive, throwing thousands out of work, who moved to cities or migrated overseas.
Land was cleared in Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia; railways, harbours and settlements needed capital from London and labour from migrants.
Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the nineteenth century, and some 150 million worldwide left their homes.
By 1890 a global agricultural economy had taken shape; in west Punjab canal colonies grew wheat and cotton for export.
Between 1820 and 1914 world trade multiplied 25 to 40 times, nearly 60 per cent of it in primary products.

subsections.title: Role of Technology
points: Railways, steamships and the telegraph were important inventions, but technological advances often resulted from social, political and economic factors such as colonisation.
Till the 1870s animals were shipped live from America to Europe, making meat an expensive luxury.
Refrigerated ships allowed animals to be slaughtered in America, Australia or New Zealand and shipped as frozen meat, lowering prices and varying the diet of Europe's poor.
Better living conditions promoted social peace at home and support for imperialism abroad.

subsections.title: Late nineteenth-century Colonialism
points: Expanding trade also meant a loss of freedoms and livelihoods for colonised societies.
In 1885 the big European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa, drawing straight borders.
Britain and France expanded their territories, Belgium and Germany became new colonial powers, and the US took over some Spanish colonies in the late 1890s.
Explorations such as Henry Morton Stanley's in Central Africa were directly linked to imperial projects.

subsections.title: Rinderpest, or the Cattle Plague
points: Africa had abundant land and livestock and a small population, so people rarely worked for wages, creating a labour shortage for European plantations and mines.
Employers imposed heavy taxes, changed inheritance laws so only one family member inherited land, and confined mineworkers in compounds.

Rinderpest arrived in the late 1880s with infected cattle from British Asia for Italian soldiers invading Eritrea, reached the Atlantic coast in 1892 and the Cape five years later, killing 90 per cent of cattle.
Colonisers monopolised the remaining cattle, forcing Africans into the labour market and subduing Africa.

subsections.title: Indentured Labour Migration from India
points: Hundreds of thousands of Indian and Chinese labourers worked on plantations, mines and construction worldwide; Indian indentured labourers were promised return travel after five years.
Most came from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu, where cottage industries declined and rents rose.
Main destinations were the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius and Fiji; Tamil migrants went to Ceylon and Malaya, and others to Assam tea gardens.
Agents gave false information; indenture has been described as a 'new system of slavery', with harsh conditions and few legal rights.
Workers created new cultural forms such as 'Hosay' in Trinidad, and Rastafarianism and 'chutney music' reflect links with Indian migrants.
Nationalist leaders opposed the system from the 1900s, and it was abolished in 1921.

subsections.title: Indian Entrepreneurs Abroad
points: Shikaripuri shroffs and Nattukottai Chettiars financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia with their own or borrowed funds.
They had a sophisticated system to transfer money over large distances and developed indigenous forms of corporate organisation.
Hyderabadi Sindhi traders established emporia at busy ports worldwide from the 1860s, selling curios to tourists.

subsections.title: Indian Trade, Colonialism and the Global System
points: Tariffs on cloth imports into Britain reduced the inflow of fine Indian cotton, and Indian textiles faced competition in other markets.
The share of cotton textiles in India's exports fell from some 30 per cent around 1800 to 15 per cent by 1815 and below 3 per cent by the 1870s.
Raw cotton exports rose from 5 to 35 per cent between 1812 and 1871; indigo and opium to China were also major exports.
Britain had a trade surplus with India, which it used to balance deficits with other countries through a multilateral settlement system, and to pay 'home charges'.

sections.title: The Inter-war Economy
points: The First World War plunged the first half of the twentieth century into a crisis that took over three decades to overcome.

subsections.title: Wartime Transformations
points: The war was fought between the Allies (Britain, France, Russia, later the US) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Turkey) and lasted more than four years.
It was the first modern industrial war, using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons; 9 million died and 20 million were injured.
Deaths reduced Europe's workforce, industries were restructured for war, and women took up jobs earlier done by men.
Britain borrowed heavily from the US, transforming the US from an international debtor into an international creditor.

subsections.title: Post-war Recovery
points: Britain faced a prolonged crisis: industries had grown in India and Japan, and it was burdened with huge external debts.
When the war boom ended, production fell and in 1921 one in every five British workers was out of work.
Wheat production in Canada, America and Australia expanded during the war; when eastern Europe revived, a glut lowered prices and deepened farmers' debt.

subsections.title: Rise of Mass Production and Consumption
points: Mass production became a characteristic of US industry in the 1920s; Henry Ford adapted a Chicago slaughterhouse's assembly line for his Detroit car plant.
The T-Model Ford was the world's first mass-produced car; Ford doubled the daily wage to $5 in January 1914 and banned trade unions.
US car production rose from 2 million in 1919 to more than 5 million in 1929, and consumer durables were bought through hire purchase.
In 1923 the US resumed exporting capital and became the largest overseas lender.

subsections.title: The Great Depression
points: The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s, with catastrophic declines in production, employment, incomes and trade; agricultural regions were worst hit.
Causes included agricultural overproduction with falling prices, and the withdrawal of US loans: over $1 billion in the first half of 1928, a quarter of that a year later.
Bank failures and collapse of currencies followed in Europe, and the US doubled import duties.
In the US over 4,000 banks had closed by 1933 and about 110,000 companies collapsed between 1929 and 1932.

subsections.title: India and the Great Depression
points: India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934, and wheat prices fell by 50 per cent.
The colonial government refused to reduce revenue demands; Bengal jute growers saw raw jute prices crash more than 60 per cent.
Peasants' indebtedness increased and India became an exporter of gold, which helped Britain's recovery but did little for the peasant.
Urban India fared better: those with fixed incomes found everything cost less, and industrial investment grew with tariff protection.

sections.title: Rebuilding a World Economy: The Post-war Era
points: The Second World War was fought between the Axis powers (Nazi Germany, Japan, Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union, the US); at least 60 million people died.
Post-war reconstruction was shaped by the US's emergence as the dominant Western power and by the dominance of the Soviet Union.

subsections.title: Post-war Settlement and the Bretton Woods Institutions
points: Two lessons were drawn: mass production needs mass consumption, which needs stable incomes and full employment ensured by government intervention; and full employment needs government control over flows of goods, capital and labour.
The framework was agreed at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944.
It set up the IMF to deal with external surpluses and deficits and the World Bank to finance reconstruction; both began operations in 1947 and the US has an effective veto.
The Bretton Woods system was based on fixed exchange rates, with currencies pegged to the dollar and the dollar anchored to gold at $35 per ounce.

subsections.title: The Early Post-war Years
points: World trade grew at over 8 per cent a year and incomes at nearly 5 per cent between 1950 and 1970.
Unemployment averaged less than 5 per cent in most industrial countries.
Developing countries invested heavily in imported modern industrial plant and equipment.

subsections.title: Decolonisation and Independence
points: Most colonies in Asia and Africa became independent within two decades after the war, but were burdened by poverty.
The IMF and World Bank shifted attention to developing countries from the late 1950s, so newly independent nations came under agencies dominated by former colonial powers.

Developing countries organised as the Group of 77 (G-77) to demand a new international economic order (NIEO): control over natural resources, more development assistance, fairer raw material prices and better market access.
Multinational corporations spread worldwide in the 1950s and 1960s, partly because high import tariffs forced them to become domestic producers.

subsections.title: End of Bretton Woods and the Beginning of ‘Globalisation’
points: From the 1960s the costs of overseas involvements weakened the US; the dollar could not hold its value against gold, and fixed exchange rates gave way to floating rates.
From the mid-1970s developing countries had to borrow from Western commercial banks, leading to debt crises, especially in Africa and Latin America.
From the late 1970s MNCs shifted production to low-wage Asian countries such as China.
Relocation of industry stimulated world trade and capital flows, and India, China and Brazil have undergone rapid economic transformation.

chapters.title: The Age of Industrialisation
chapters.overview: The chapter questions the image of industrialisation as simply a story of machines and progress. It looks first at Britain – proto-industrialisation, the coming of factories, the slow pace of change and the continued importance of hand labour – and then at colonial India, where textile weavers declined under Company control and Manchester imports, factories came up, and small-scale production continued to predominate. It ends with how markets for goods were created through advertising.

sections.title: The Age of Industrialisation
points: Images such as 'Dawn of the Century' (1900) and 'Two Magicians' (1901) glorified machines and technology as signs of progress.
In such accounts the history of industrialisation becomes simply a story of development and the modern age a time of technological progress.
The chapter looks at Britain, the first industrial nation, and India, where industrial change was conditioned by colonial rule.

sections.title: Before the Industrial Revolution
points: Before factories, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market, which historians call proto-industrialisation.
In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries merchants moved to the countryside because powerful urban crafts and trade guilds restricted new entrants in towns.
Poor peasants and cottagers, losing common lands to enclosure, took merchants' advances to produce goods while continuing to cultivate small plots.
A merchant clothier bought wool from a stapler and sent it through spinners, weavers, fullers and dyers, with finishing done in London.
Each merchant employed 20 to 25 workers at each stage, so each clothier controlled hundreds of workers.

subsections.title: The Coming Up of the Factory
points: The earliest factories in England came up by the 1730s, but they multiplied only in the late eighteenth century.
Cotton was the first symbol of the new era: raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787.
Inventions increased the efficacy of carding, twisting, spinning and rolling, and Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill.
In the mill all processes were brought under one roof and management, allowing supervision, quality control and regulation of labour.

subsections.title: The Pace of Industrial Change
points: Cotton led industrialisation up to the 1840s, then iron and steel; by 1873 Britain exported iron and steel worth about £77 million, double its cotton exports.
New industries could not easily displace traditional ones: even at the end of the nineteenth century less than 20 per cent of the workforce was in technologically advanced sectors.
Traditional industries grew through small innovations in food processing, building, pottery, glass work, tanning and furniture making.
Technological change was slow: James Watt patented his improved steam engine in 1781, but at the start of the nineteenth century there were no more than 321 steam engines in England.
The typical mid-nineteenth-century worker was a traditional craftsperson and labourer, not a machine operator.

sections.title: Hand Labour and Steam Power
points: In Victorian Britain there was plenty of labour and wages were low, so industrialists did not want costly machines that replaced workers.
In seasonal industries such as gas works, breweries, bookbinding and ship repair, industrialists preferred hand labour employed for the season.
Many products needed hand labour: in mid-nineteenth-century Britain, 500 varieties of hammers and 45 kinds of axes were produced.
The upper classes preferred handmade goods as symbols of refinement, while machine-made goods were exported to colonies.
In countries with labour shortage, such as nineteenth-century America, industrialists were keen on mechanical power.

subsections.title: Life of the Workers
points: Getting a job depended on networks of friends and kin; many job-seekers waited weeks, sleeping under bridges or in Night Refuges and Casual Wards.
Seasonal work meant prolonged unemployment; wages rose somewhat but real wages fell when prices rose during the Napoleonic War.
About 10 per cent of the urban population were extremely poor, and in slumps like the 1830s unemployment rose to between 35 and 75 per cent in different regions.
Fear of unemployment made workers hostile to new technology; women who lived by hand spinning attacked the Spinning Jenny.
After the 1840s building activity in cities expanded employment, and transport workers doubled in the 1840s and again in the next 30 years.

sections.title: Industrialisation in the Colonies
points: The section looks at how a colony industrialises, including the non-mechanised sector, focusing on textiles.

subsections.title: The Age of Indian Textiles
points: Before machine industries, Indian silk and cotton goods dominated the international textile market.
Goods went overland via the north-west frontier to Afghanistan, Persia and Central Asia, and by sea through Surat, Masulipatam and Hoogly.
Indian merchants and bankers financed production; supply merchants gave advances to weavers and brokers negotiated prices at ports.
By the 1750s this network was breaking down as European companies gained monopoly rights; trade through Surat slumped from Rs 16 million in the late seventeenth century to Rs 3 million by the 1740s.
Bombay and Calcutta grew as Surat and Hoogly decayed, a sign of growing colonial power.

subsections.title: What Happened to Weavers?
points: After gaining political power in Bengal and Carnatic in the 1760s and 1770s, the East India Company asserted a monopoly right to trade.
It appointed paid servants called gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine quality.
Through a system of advances, weavers who took loans had to hand their cloth to the gomastha and could not sell to others.
Gomasthas were outsiders who acted arrogantly and punished weavers; prices paid were miserably low.
Weavers in Carnatic and Bengal deserted villages, revolted, or refused loans and took to agricultural labour.

subsections.title: Manchester Comes to India
points: Piece-goods fell from 33 per cent of India's exports in 1811-12 to no more than 3 per cent by 1850-51.
British industrialists pressed for import duties in Britain and for the Company to sell British manufactures in India.
Cotton piece-goods were over 31 per cent of the value of Indian imports by 1850 and over 50 per cent by the 1870s.
Weavers lost both export and local markets; in the 1860s the American Civil War raised raw cotton prices, and by the end of the century Indian factories flooded the market.

sections.title: Factories Come Up
points: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854 and began production two years later; by 1862 four mills had 94,000 spindles and 2,150 looms.
The first jute mill in Bengal was set up in 1855 and another in 1862; the Elgin Mill in Kanpur started in the 1860s, and the first spinning and weaving mill of Madras began production by 1874.

subsections.title: The Early Entrepreneurs
points: Many business groups made their money in the China trade: Dwarkanath Tagore set up six joint-stock companies in the 1830s and 1840s.
Parsis like Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata built industrial empires partly from exports to China and raw cotton to England.
Seth Hukumchand set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917; G.D. Birla's father and grandfather also traded with China.
Indian merchants were barred from trading with Europe in manufactured goods and edged out of shipping.
Till the First World War European Managing Agencies such as Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule and Jardine Skinner & Co. controlled a large sector of Indian industry.

subsections.title: Where Did the Workers Come From?
points: Factory workers numbered 584,000 in 1901 and over 2,436,000 by 1946.
Most workers came from nearby districts: over 50 per cent of Bombay cotton workers in 1911 came from Ratnagiri; many moved between village and city.
Jobs were scarce, and industrialists employed a jobber, often an old trusted worker, who recruited from his village and came to demand money and gifts.

sections.title: The Peculiarities of Industrial Growth
points: European Managing Agencies invested in tea and coffee plantations, mining, indigo and jute, mainly for export.
Early Indian cotton mills produced coarse yarn rather than fabric to avoid competing with Manchester, selling to handloom weavers or China.
The swadeshi movement, tariff demands and falling yarn exports to China from 1906 led industrialists to shift to cloth; piece-goods production doubled between 1900 and 1912.
During the First World War Manchester imports declined and Indian factories supplied war needs; afterwards Manchester never recaptured its position.

subsections.title: Small-scale Industries Predominate
points: Large industries formed a small segment of the economy, about 67 per cent of them in Bengal and Bombay in 1911.
Only 5 per cent of the industrial labour force worked in registered factories in 1911 and 10 per cent in 1931.
Handloom cloth production almost trebled between 1900 and 1940, helped by technologies like the fly shuttle; by 1941 over 35 per cent of handlooms had fly shuttles.
Weavers of finer cloth for the well-to-do and of specialised weaves such as Banarasi and Baluchari saris survived better than those of coarse cloth.
Craftspeople who expanded production lived hard lives, but their labour was integral to industrialisation.

sections.title: Market for Goods
points: New consumers were created through advertisements, which make products appear desirable and necessary.
Manchester industrialists put labels such as 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' on cloth bundles as a mark of quality.
Labels carried images of Indian gods and goddesses to give divine approval and make foreign goods appear familiar.
Calendars, used even by people who could not read, and figures of emperors and nawabs popularised products.
Indian manufacturers used advertisements to carry the nationalist message of swadeshi.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: The age of industries brought major technological changes, factories and a new industrial labour force.
Hand technology and small-scale production remained an important part of the industrial landscape.

chapters.title: Print Culture and the Modern World
chapters.overview: The chapter traces the history of print from its beginnings in East Asia to its expansion in Europe and India. It explains Gutenberg's press and the print revolution, the new reading public, religious debates and the fear of print, the link with the Enlightenment and French Revolution, nineteenth-century readers and innovations, and in India the coming of print, religious reform debates, new forms of publication, women and the poor as readers, and colonial censorship.

sections.title: The First Printed Books
points: The earliest print technology was hand printing developed in China, Japan and Korea; from AD 594 books in China were printed by rubbing paper against inked woodblocks.
The Chinese 'accordion book' was folded and stitched at the side, and skilled craftsmen duplicated the beauty of calligraphy.
The imperial state was long the major producer of print, printing textbooks for civil service examinations.
By the seventeenth century merchants used print, reading became a leisure activity, and women read and published poetry and plays.
Western mechanical presses came in the late nineteenth century, and Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture.

subsections.title: Print in Japan
points: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing into Japan around AD 768-770.
The book states that the oldest Chinese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra with six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.
In medieval Japan books were cheap and abundant; in late eighteenth-century Edo illustrated collections depicted urban culture.
Kitagawa Utamaro, born in Edo in 1753, was known for ukiyo ('pictures of the floating world') prints that influenced Manet, Monet and Van Gogh.

sections.title: Print Comes to Europe
points: Chinese paper reached Europe via the silk route in the eleventh century; in 1295 Marco Polo brought knowledge of woodblock printing back to Italy.
Luxury editions were still handwritten on vellum for aristocrats, while merchants and students bought cheaper printed copies.
Booksellers employed scribes, often more than 50 for one bookseller, but handwritten manuscripts could not meet demand as they were expensive, laborious and fragile.
By the early fifteenth century woodblocks printed textiles, playing cards and religious pictures, and in the 1430s Johann Gutenberg developed the first-known printing press at Strasbourg.

subsections.title: Gutenberg and the Printing Press
points: Gutenberg drew on his knowledge of olive presses and lead moulds: the olive press was the model for the printing press and moulds cast metal types.
By 1448 he perfected the system; the first book he printed was the Bible, about 180 copies over three years.
Early printed books resembled manuscripts, with borders illuminated and illustrations painted by hand.
Between 1450 and 1550 printing presses spread across Europe; 20 million copies were printed in the second half of the fifteenth century and about 200 million in the sixteenth.
The shift from hand printing to mechanical printing led to the print revolution.

sections.title: The Print Revolution and Its Impact
points: The print revolution transformed people's relationship to information, knowledge, institutions and authorities.

subsections.title: A New Reading Public
points: Printing reduced the cost of books, and a new reading public emerged where there had been a hearing public living in an oral culture.
As literacy was low, printers published illustrated popular ballads and folk tales that were sung and recited in villages and taverns.
Oral culture entered print and printed material was orally transmitted, blurring the line between hearing and reading publics.

subsections.title: Religious Debates and the Fear of Print
points: Print allowed wide circulation of ideas, even from those who disagreed with established authorities.
Religious authorities, monarchs, writers and artists feared that uncontrolled printing would spread rebellious and irreligious thoughts.
In 1517 Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising the Roman Catholic Church; its wide reproduction led to the Protestant Reformation.
Luther's translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies in a few weeks; he called printing 'the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one'.

subsections.title: Print and Dissent
points: Print stimulated individual interpretations of faith even among little-educated people.
In the sixteenth century Menocchio, an Italian miller, reinterpreted the Bible and was executed by the Roman Church's inquisition.
The Roman Church imposed controls on publishers and booksellers and maintained an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.
Erasmus, in Adages (1508), expressed anxiety that swarms of books would make even valuable publications lose their value.

sections.title: The Reading Mania
points: Literacy rose in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries as churches set up village schools; by the end of the eighteenth century it reached 60 to 80 per cent in some parts of Europe.
Pedlars sold almanacs, ballads and folktales; in England penny chapbooks were sold by chapmen, and in France the low-priced 'Biliotheque Bleue' circulated.
The periodical press developed from the early eighteenth century, combining current affairs with entertainment.
Ideas of scientists like Isaac Newton and thinkers such as Thomas Paine, Voltaire and Rousseau became accessible to common people.

subsections.title: Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world!
points: By the mid-eighteenth century many believed books could spread progress and liberate society from despotism.
Novelist Louise-Sebastien Mercier declared the printing press 'the most powerful engine of progress'.
Mercier proclaimed: 'Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtual writer!'

subsections.title: Print Culture and the French Revolution
points: First argument: print popularised Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau, who attacked the Church and despotism and argued for reason.
Second: print created a new culture of dialogue and debate in which values and institutions were re-evaluated.
Third: by the 1780s literature mocking royalty and its morality circulated underground and fed hostility to the monarchy.
Yet people also read monarchical and Church propaganda and interpreted things their own way; print did not directly shape minds but opened the possibility of thinking differently.

sections.title: The Nineteenth Century
points: The nineteenth century saw vast leaps in mass literacy in Europe, bringing new readers among children, women and workers.

subsections.title: Children, Women and Workers
points: As primary education became compulsory, school textbooks became critical; a children's press was set up in France in 1857.
The Grimm Brothers' 1812 collection edited out material thought unsuitable for children, so print recorded old tales but also changed them.
Penny magazines and manuals were meant for women; novelists like Jane Austen, the Bronte sisters and George Eliot defined a new type of woman.
Lending libraries educated white-collar workers, artisans and lower-middle-class people, and workers wrote political tracts and autobiographies.

subsections.title: Further Innovations
points: By the late eighteenth century presses were made of metal; by the mid-nineteenth century Richard M. Hoe perfected the power-driven cylindrical press printing 8,000 sheets per hour.
The offset press of the late nineteenth century printed up to six colours at a time, and electrically operated presses followed.
Periodicals serialised novels; the Shilling Series appeared in 1920s England, and the dust cover is a twentieth-century innovation.
During the Great Depression of the 1930s publishers brought out cheap paperback editions.

sections.title: India and the World of Print
points: The section looks at when printing began in India and how ideas were written before print.

subsections.title: Manuscripts Before the Age of Print
points: India had a rich tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and vernacular languages, copied on palm leaves or handmade paper.
Manuscripts were expensive, fragile and written in varied scripts, so not widely used in everyday life.
In pre-colonial Bengal's village schools students learnt to write from dictation and many became literate without reading texts.

subsections.title: Print Comes to India
points: The printing press came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century; by 1674 about 50 books were printed in Konkani and Kanara.
Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in 1713; by 1710 Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts.
From 1780 James Augustus Hickey edited the Bengal Gazette; Warren Hastings persecuted him for gossip about Company officials.
The first Indian newspaper was the weekly Bengal Gazette brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

sections.title: Religious Reform and Public Debates
points: From the early nineteenth century religious debates were carried out in print, and printed tracts and newspapers shaped the debate for a wider public.

Reformers and Hindu orthodoxy clashed over widow immolation, monotheism, Brahmanical priesthood and idolatry; Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821 and the orthodoxy commissioned the Samachar Chandrika.
From 1822 two Persian newspapers (Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar) and the Gujarati Bombay Samachar appeared.
North Indian ulama used cheap lithographic presses; the Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands of fatwas.
The first printed Ramcharitmanas came from Calcutta in 1810; the Naval Kishore Press and Shri Venkateshwar Press published vernacular religious texts, and newspapers created pan-Indian identities.

sections.title: New Forms of Publication
points: Readers wanted to see their own lives reflected; the novel acquired distinctively Indian forms, along with lyrics, short stories and essays.
By the end of the nineteenth century a new visual culture emerged; Raja Ravi Varma produced images for mass circulation and cheap prints and calendars reached the poor.
By the 1870s caricatures and cartoons in journals commented on social and political issues, both imperial and nationalist.

subsections.title: Women and Print
points: Women's reading increased in middle-class homes; journals carried writings by women and explained why women should be educated.

Conservative Hindus and Muslims opposed women's education, but some women defied them; Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly and wrote Amar Jiban (1876), the first full-length autobiography in Bengali.
Kailashbashini Debi wrote about women's experiences from the 1860s, and Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai wrote about upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows, in the 1880s.
Hindi printing began seriously from the 1870s, much of it devoted to women's education; in Punjab Ram Chaddha's Istri Dharm Vichar taught obedience.
The Battala area of central Calcutta printed popular books, which pedlars took to homes for women to read.

subsections.title: Print and the Poor People
points: Cheap small books were sold at crossroads in Madras towns, and public libraries were set up from the early twentieth century.
Jyotiba Phule wrote about caste injustice in Gulamgiri (1871); B.R. Ambedkar and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar) wrote powerfully on caste.
Kanpur millworker Kashibaba published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938 linking caste and class exploitation; Sudarshan Chakr's poems were collected in Sacchi Kavitayan.
By the 1930s Bangalore cotton millworkers set up libraries, following Bombay workers.

sections.title: Print and Censorship
points: Before 1798 the Company was little concerned with censorship; early controls targeted Englishmen critical of Company misrule.
By the 1820s the Calcutta Supreme Court regulated press freedom; in 1835 Bentinck agreed to revise press laws and Thomas Macaulay restored earlier freedoms.
After the revolt of 1857 attitudes changed, and the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, modelled on the Irish Press Laws, gave extensive rights to censor the vernacular press.
Nationalist newspapers grew despite repression; Tilak's sympathetic writing in Kesari about deported Punjab revolutionaries led to his imprisonment in 1908.
During the First World War 22 newspapers had to furnish securities under the Defence of India Rules and 18 shut down; in August 1942 about 90 newspapers were suppressed.

keyTerms.meaning: The art of beautiful and stylised writing.
A parchment made from the skin of animals.
In letterpress printing, a board pressed onto the back of the paper to get the impression from the type; once wooden, later steel.
The person who composes the text for printing.
Metal frame in which types are laid and the text composed.
A historical account or folk tale in verse, usually sung or recited.
Places where people gathered to drink alcohol, be served food, meet friends and exchange news.
A sixteenth-century movement to reform the Catholic Church dominated by Rome; Martin Luther was one of the main reformers.
A former Roman Catholic court for identifying and punishing heretics.
Beliefs which do not follow the accepted teachings of the Church; heretical beliefs were severely punished.
The state of being fulfilled much beyond the point of satisfaction.
Action, speech or writing that is seen as opposing the government.
Sub groups within a religion.
An annual publication giving astronomical data, movements of the sun and moon, timing of tides and eclipses, and other everyday information.
Pocket-size books sold by travelling pedlars called chapmen, popular from the sixteenth-century print revolution.
A system of governance in which absolute power is exercised by an individual, unregulated by legal and constitutional checks.
Legal scholars of Islam and the sharia.
A legal pronouncement on Islamic law usually given by a mufti to clarify issues on which the law is uncertain.
'Pictures of the floating world', an art form depicting ordinary, especially urban, human experiences.

keyResults.label: AD 594
keyResults.statement: Books in China printed by rubbing paper against inked woodblocks.

keyResults.label: AD 768-770
keyResults.statement: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing into Japan.

keyResults.label: AD 868
keyResults.statement: The Buddhist Diamond Sutra printed.
Marco Polo returned to Italy from China with knowledge of woodblock printing.

keyResults.label: 1430s
keyResults.statement: Johann Gutenberg developed the first-known printing press at Strasbourg.
Gutenberg perfected his system; his Bible, about 180 copies, took three years.

keyResults.label: Gutenberg press
keyResults.statement: Could print 250 sheets on one side per hour.

keyResults.label: Book production in Europe
keyResults.statement: 20 million copies in the second half of the fifteenth century; about 200 million in the sixteenth century.
Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses.
The Roman Church began maintaining an Index of Prohibited Books.
Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book at Cochin.
First Malayalam book printed.
James Augustus Hickey began editing the Bengal Gazette.
First printed edition of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta.
Rammohun Roy began publishing the Sambad Kaumudi.
Governor-General Bentinck agreed to revise press laws; Macaulay restored earlier freedoms.
A children's press set up in France.
Deoband Seminary founded.
Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri.
Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban published, the first full-length autobiography in Bengali.

keyResults.label: Vernacular Press Act (1878)
keyResults.statement: Modelled on the Irish Press Laws; gave the government extensive rights to censor the vernacular press.
Balgangadhar Tilak imprisoned for writing in Kesari about deported Punjab revolutionaries.

keyResults.label: August 1942
keyResults.statement: About 90 newspapers suppressed under the Defence of India Act.

keyResults.label: Richard M. Hoe's cylindrical press
keyResults.statement: Power-driven press of the mid-nineteenth century printing 8,000 sheets per hour.

You are a bookseller advertising the availability of new cheap printed books. Design a poster for your shop window.
Imagine that you are a cartoonist in France before the revolution. Design a cartoon as it would have appeared in a pamphlet.
